Now we create the class.

Code 
class LayerNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, emb_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = 1e-5 
        self.scale = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(emb_dim)) 
        self.shift = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(emb_dim))

    def forward(self,x):
        mean = x.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        var = x.var(dim=-1, keepdim=True, unbiased=False) 
        norm_x = (x-mean)/torch.sqrt(var + self.eps)
        return self.scale*norm_x + self.shift

3 Implementing a Feed-Forward Network with GELU Activations

GELU stands for Gaussian Error Linear Unit. It looks similar to ReLU (), but mathematically, it is the product of and the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a standard normal distribution:

GELU is like a “confidence booster.” If is high, confidence is high, and the CDF multiplies it by nearly 1. If is low, the model is less confident, and the CDF multiplies it by a smaller number.

Code 
class GELU(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
    
    def forward(self,x):
        return 0.5 * x * (1 + torch.tanh(
            torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(2/torch.pi))* (x + 0.044715 * torch.pow(x,3))
        ))

Now we implement the feed-forward neural network.

Code 
class FeedForward(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self,cfg):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(cfg["emb_dim"],4*cfg["emb_dim"]),
            GELU(),
            nn.Linear(4*cfg["emb_dim"], cfg["emb_dim"])
        )

    def forward(self,x):
        return self.layers(x)

4 Adding Shortcut Connections

Shortcut (or Skip/Residual) connections mitigate vanishing gradients. They create an alternative path for the gradient to flow by skipping one or more layers, adding the output of one layer to the output of a later layer.

Code 
class ExampleDeepNeuralNetwork(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, layer_sizes, use_shortcut):
        super().__init__()
        self.use_shortcut = use_shortcut
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([
            nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(layer_sizes[0], layer_sizes[1]), GELU()),
            nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(layer_sizes[1], layer_sizes[2]), GELU()),
            nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(layer_sizes[2], layer_sizes[3]), GELU()),
            nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(layer_sizes[3], layer_sizes[4]), GELU()),
            nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(layer_sizes[4], layer_sizes[5]), GELU())
        ])

    def forward(self,x):
        for layer in self.layers:
            layer_output = layer(x)
            if self.use_shortcut and x.shape == layer_output.shape:
                x = x + layer_output
            else:
                x = layer_output
        return x

5 Connecting Attention & Linear Layers in Transformer Blocks

We have now captured all the components of the GPT-2 architecture. Let’s fill in the actual TransformerBlock:

Code 
from attention import MultiHeadAttention 

class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cfg):
        super().__init__()
        self.att = MultiHeadAttention(
            d_in = cfg["emb_dim"],
            d_out = cfg["emb_dim"],
            context_length = cfg["context_length"],
            num_heads = cfg["n_heads"],
            dropout = cfg['drop_rate'],
            qkv_bias = cfg["qkv_bias"]
        ) 

        self.ff = FeedForward(cfg) 
        self.norm1 = LayerNorm(cfg["emb_dim"])
        self.norm2 = LayerNorm(cfg["emb_dim"])
        self.drop_shortcut = nn.Dropout(cfg["drop_rate"])

    def forward(self,x):
        # MHA section
        shortcut = x
        x = self.norm1(x) 
        x = self.att(x) 
        x = self.drop_shortcut(x) 
        x = x + shortcut 
        
        # Feedforward section
        shortcut = x 
        x = self.norm2(x) 
        x = self.ff(x) 
        x = self.drop_shortcut(x)
        x = x + shortcut 
        return x

6 Coding the GPT Model

Time to stitch everything together.

Code 
class GPTModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cfg):
        super().__init__()
        self.tok_emb = nn.Embedding(cfg["vocab_size"],cfg["emb_dim"])
        self.pos_emb = nn.Embedding(cfg["context_length"],cfg["emb_dim"])
        self.drop_emb = nn.Dropout(cfg["drop_rate"])

        self.trf_blocks = nn.Sequential(
            *[TransformerBlock(cfg) for _ in range(cfg["n_layers"])]
        )
        self.final_norm = LayerNorm(cfg["emb_dim"])
        self.out_head = nn.Linear(
            cfg["emb_dim"],cfg["vocab_size"],bias=False
        )

    def forward(self,in_idx):
        batch_size, seq_len = in_idx.shape
        tok_embeds = self.tok_emb(in_idx)
        pos_embeds = self.pos_emb(torch.arange(seq_len, device=in_idx.device))
        x = tok_embeds + pos_embeds
        x = self.drop_emb(x)
        x = self.trf_blocks(x)
        x = self.final_norm(x)
        logits = self.out_head(x)
        return logits

7 Generating Text

The model converts input text to an output tensor. We now need to generate text by selecting tokens based on probability distributions.

Code 
def generate_text_simple(model,idx,max_new_tokens,context_size): 
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
        idx_cond = idx[:,-context_size:] 
        with torch.no_grad():
            logits = model(idx_cond) 
        
        logits = logits[:,-1,:] 
        probas = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
        idx_next = torch.argmax(probas, dim=-1, keepdim=True) 
        idx = torch.cat((idx,idx_next), dim=1) 

    return idx

8 Summarizing Thoughts

In this chapter, we implemented the full end-to-end architecture of a GPT-2 model. As we’ve seen, GPT has multiple moving parts from an architectural standpoint that must work in harmony.

We started by defining a configuration file that serves as the blueprint. From there, we built the Transformer block, which houses the two primary engines: Multi-Head Attention and Feed-Forward networks. We also explored how deep networks are prone to vanishing or exploding gradients and saw how techniques like Shortcut Connections, Layer Normalization, and GELU activations work in tandem to stop this phenomenon. Finally, we learned to decode the output text using the tokenizer.

8.1 Perhaps in the next blog, we can go top-down on the GPT-2 architecture or dive into one of the foundational papers.

item.title: Under the Hood of the First Phase 3 Personalized Cancer Vaccine
item.dc:creator: Pratyush Sinha
item.description:
Let’s start with the actual announcement.

A few weeks ago, Merck and Moderna released a clinical update that sent a jolt of genuine excitement through the oncology world:

“Merck and Moderna Announce Phase 3 INTerpath-001 Trial of Intismeran Autogene Plus KEYTRUDA® Met Endpoints of Recurrence-Free Survival (RFS) and Distant Metastasis-Free Survival (DMFS) in Patients With Completely Resected Stage IIB-IV Melanoma”

If you don’t read clinical press releases for a living, that headline looks like a wall of biotech alphabet soup. But behind those acronyms is a genuinely historic milestone: for the first time in medical history, an individualized cancer vaccine—designed by computers specifically for each patient’s unique tumor—has succeeded in a definitive Phase 3 trial.

Before diving into how this incredible machine works, let’s translate what this news actually means in plain English.

What the News Actually Means (In Plain Terms)

To understand why doctors and scientists are so excited, we need to look at what happens to a patient diagnosed with high-risk melanoma:

1. The Real Danger: Stage IV and Metastasis

Melanoma is an aggressive form of skin cancer. When solid tumors are diagnosed, doctors assign them a stage from I to IV. You don’t need to memorize the intricacies of every intermediate stage, but here is the critical rule: Stage IV is the most dangerous stage in oncology.

Why? Because Stage IV means distant metastasis—the cancer cells have broken away from the skin, traveled through the bloodstream or lymphatic vessels, and colonized distant vital organs like the lungs, liver, bones, or brain. Once cancer metastasizes widely to vital organs, it becomes exponentially harder to treat and frequently fatal.

2. The Illusion of “Clean Margins” & Dormant Micrometastases

When a patient has high-risk melanoma (Stages IIB through IV), a surgeon cuts out the visible tumor. If the pathology report comes back showing “complete surgical resection” with “clean margins,” it means the surgeon got all the cancer they could physically see.

Here is the catch: surgery rarely clears 100% of the cells.

Long before surgery, microscopic clusters of malignant cells—known as dormant micrometastases—often detach and drift invisibly into circulation. These clusters are far too small to show up on CT or PET scans. Left alone, they can sit quietly for months or even years, only to “wake up” later and seed deadly metastatic tumors.

3. The Role of Adjuvant Therapy

This brings us to adjuvant therapy. Adjuvant treatment is therapy given after surgery to act as an insurance policy. Its sole job is to hunt down and eliminate those invisible dormant micrometastases before they can take root.

[Surgery: Primary Tumor Removed] ──> [Invisible Micrometastases Linger in Body]
                                                  │
                   ┌──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┐
                   ▼                                                             ▼
       [Standard Adjuvant Care]                                    [Personalized Vaccine + Keytruda]
         Keytruda alone blocks                                      Keytruda unblocks the immune system 
        cancer's defense switches                                   WHILE custom mRNA directs T-cells
                                                                    to hunt specific tumor mutations

4. The Trial Yardsticks: RFS vs. DMFS

The Phase 3 trial (INTerpath-001) tested whether adding Moderna’s custom vaccine to Merck’s standard immunotherapy (Keytruda) could stop these micrometastases better than Keytruda alone:

  • Recurrence-Free Survival (RFS): Did the cancer stay away, or did it return locally or in nearby lymph nodes?
  • Distant Metastasis-Free Survival (DMFS): Did the cancer spread to distant vital organs like the lungs, liver, or brain?

The result? The combination met both endpoints with high statistical significance. Adding the custom mRNA vaccine significantly improved the odds of staying cancer-free and stopped the disease from spreading to distant organs compared to the world’s best standard-of-care drug.

Peeling the Onion: The Two Core Dimensions

The reason this breakthrough matters far beyond melanoma is that it isn’t just a lucky chemical compound—it is an entirely new engineering paradigm.

To understand how Moderna and Merck actually pulled this off, we can look at the system across two core dimensions:

  1. The Physical & Biological Machine: The 6-week relay from surgical biopsy to custom vial, and why the vaccine needs Keytruda as an accomplice.
  2. The Personalization Challenge: Why cancer is fundamentally an problem, and why human biology couldn’t solve this without machine learning.

Let’s start with the physical journey inside the clinic.

Part 1: The Physical Machine (From Biopsy to Bespoke Vial)

Building a personalized vaccine is a race against biological time. After surgery, the patient has an adjuvant window of roughly 6 to 8 weeks. Wait longer, and those dormant micrometastases have time to establish protective biological shields that are far harder to eradicate.

Within those six weeks, the medical and engineering teams execute a continuous physical loop:

[1. Biopsy & Blood Sample] ──> [2. High-Throughput NGS Sequencing]
                                              │
                                              ▼
[4. Cell-Free mRNA Synthesis] <── [3. In Silico AI Target Selection]
              │
              ▼
[5. LNP Encapsulation] ──> [6. Intramuscular Injection & T-Cell Training]

To understand this loop, let’s first clarify a few foundational terms that often get blurred together:

  • Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS): Traditional DNA sequencing was slow and read one gene at a time. High-throughput NGS is modern industrial sequencing technology that reads billions of DNA and RNA letters simultaneously in parallel. It allows researchers to sequence an entire human genome in hours instead of years, giving us a complete digital readout of the patient’s tumor.
  • Neoantigen vs. mRNA (The “Wanted Poster” vs. The “Instruction Tape”):
    • An antigen is any molecular flag the immune system can recognize. A neoantigen (new antigen) is a mutated protein fragment produced exclusively by cancer cells. Healthy cells do not have it. It is the molecular “wanted poster” or bullseye.
    • mRNA (Messenger RNA) is the temporary genetic blueprint. The vaccine does not inject physical neoantigen proteins. Instead, it injects synthetic mRNA code that instructs the patient’s own cells to manufacture those neoantigens temporarily, showing the immune system exactly what the cancer looks like.
  • T-Cells (CD8+ Cytotoxic & CD4+ Helper): The elite soldiers of the immune system. CD8+ “killer” T-cells can physically inspect other cells and inject lethal toxins into any cell displaying a foreign target.

The Dual Mechanism: The Gas Pedal and the Brake

To understand why this combination works, we first need to answer an obvious question: how does Keytruda work on its own when there is no mRNA vaccine?

How Keytruda Works Alone (Releasing Pre-Existing T-Cells)

Your immune system is not entirely blind to cancer. In many patients, a small squad of T-cells naturally stumbles upon the tumor, recognizes a mutated protein, and attempts to attack. These are known as Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocytes (TILs).

However, cancer cells quickly adapt. To defend themselves, tumors display a surface protein called PD-L1. When PD-L1 connects with the PD-1 receptor on an attacking T-cell, it acts as a molecular handbrake, flipping a biochemical “off-switch” that puts the T-cell into a state of exhaustion and paralysis. The T-cells are physically present at the tumor, but their weapons are locked.

Keytruda (pembrolizumab) is a monoclonal antibody that caps the PD-1 receptor on T-cells. By physically blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 connection, Keytruda prevents the cancer from engaging that off-switch. It releases the emergency brake, re-invigorating those exhausted, pre-existing T-cells so they can resume fighting.

How Keytruda Works Alone:
[Pre-existing, Exhausted T-Cells] ──(Keytruda Blocks PD-1)──> [T-Cells Re-awaken & Attack]
* Catch: Relies entirely on whatever random T-cells the patient happens to already have.

Why Keytruda Alone Hits a Ceiling

Keytruda revolutionized oncology, but on its own, it has a fundamental limitation: it relies on luck.

Keytruda cannot create new T-cells or choose what they target. It can only unchain the T-cells that the patient’s body has already generated naturally. If a patient has very few tumor-reactive T-cells, or if their natural T-cells are aimed at weak targets, releasing the brake achieves very little.

Furthermore, in the post-surgical (adjuvant) setting, the surgeon has already removed the primary tumor mass. Without a large tumor constantly stimulating the immune system, there are very few naturally active T-cells circulating to hunt down microscopic remnants.

Why the Personalized Vaccine Completes the Circuit

This is where Moderna’s mRNA vaccine transforms the equation:

Step 1: The Gas Pedal (Moderna mRNA Vaccine)
Does not rely on luck. Actively manufactures a brand-new, massive army 
of millions of T-cells trained specifically on up to 34 tumor mutations.

Step 2: Releasing the Brake (Keytruda Anti-PD-1)
Ensures that when these newly minted T-cells reach surviving cancer 
cells, the tumor cannot use PD-L1 to switch them off.
  • The mRNA Vaccine acts as the Gas Pedal: Instead of hoping the immune system notices the cancer, the vaccine delivers a clear intelligence briefing. It forces dendritic cells to present up to 34 mathematically optimized tumor neoantigens, triggering massive clonal expansion of fresh, high-affinity killer T-cells.
  • Keytruda acts as Releasing the Brake: As this newly trained army circulates to hunt down dormant micrometastases, Keytruda ensures the cancer’s PD-L1 shield cannot disarm them.

Giving Keytruda alone is like taking your foot off the brake in a car with an empty gas tank—the car is free to move, but there is no engine driving it forward. Giving the vaccine alone is like stepping on the gas with the emergency brake locked.

Used together, the vaccine builds and accelerates the engine, while Keytruda removes the brake.

Why mRNA Beats DNA and Peptides

To deliver up to 34 personalized targets within the 6-week surgical window, the choice of biological delivery vehicle is decisive:

Modality Where It Operates Genomic Integration Hazard Manufacturing Turnaround 34-Target Scalability
DNA Plasmids Cell Nucleus Yes (Theoretical risk of inserting into host genome) 4–6 Weeks High engineering friction
Synthetic Peptides Extracellular None 4–9 Months Chemically prohibitive (34 separate syntheses)
mRNA (Moderna) Cytoplasm Zero (Cannot enter human genome) 2–3 Weeks Single continuous digital sequence

Synthetic peptides were the historical standard in experimental cancer vaccines. But synthesizing 34 distinct peptide chains for a single patient requires 34 separate chemical syntheses, purifications, and quality-control runs. Because peptides vary radically in solubility, charge, and chemical stability, batch failures across 34 simultaneous reactions make a 6-week turnaround impossible.

mRNA solved this by standardizing the physical chemistry.

Whether an mRNA strand codes for neoantigen A or neoantigen B, its chemical properties are virtually identical. The synthesis machinery, purification columns, and lipid nanoparticle formulation remain invariant. The factory operates like a digital compiler: the physical hardware stays the same, and only the digital sequence sent to the synthesizer changes.

Part 2: The Personalization Engine (Why This Demands AI)

If the biological blueprint is this clean, why couldn’t we build this twenty years ago?

Because between the patient’s DNA sequencing files and the mRNA synthesizer lies an overwhelming biological puzzle: cancer is fundamentally an problem.

       [Tumor Biopsy] ──> 1,000+ Raw Somatic Mutations
                                  │
                                  ▼  (Filter 1: Active RNA Expression)
                          300-500 Expressed Transcripts
                                  │
                                  ▼  (Filter 2: HLA Presentation)
                           20-50 Displayed on Surface
                                  │
                                  ▼  (Filter 3: TCR Immunogenicity)
                         Top 34 Potent Neoantigens

The Lock and Key: Mutations vs. HLA Diversity

Melanoma carries an enormous number of mutations caused by ultraviolet sun damage. A single biopsy typically reveals hundreds or thousands of DNA alterations.

However, a mutation deep inside a cancer cell is completely invisible to passing T-cells. For the immune system to see it, the cell must chop the mutated protein into short peptide fragments (8–11 amino acids long) and display them on surface presentation platters called Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) molecules (part of the Major Histocompatibility Complex, or MHC).

Here is the computational wall:

  • Extreme Genetic Diversity: HLA genes are the most polymorphic genes in the human genome, with tens of thousands of known allele variants across humanity.
  • The Unique Molecular Pocket: Every person inherits a unique combination of HLA alleles. Each HLA molecule forms a physical pocket with distinct chemical charges and anchor points.
  • Zero Transferability: A mutation that fits perfectly into Patient A’s HLA-A*02:01 pocket will be completely ignored by Patient B’s HLA-A*24:02 pocket.

You cannot manufacture an “off-the-shelf” melanoma vaccine because a target that cures one patient is invisible in another.

The Needle in the Haystack

From that initial pool of ~1,000 mutations in a patient’s tumor:

  1. Only 30–50% are actively transcribed into RNA at levels high enough to matter.
  2. Less than 2% of those expressed peptides have the exact biochemical geometry to bind the patient’s specific HLA molecules and reach the outer cell surface.
  3. Less than 20% of presented peptides look sufficiently “foreign” to stimulate a T-cell receptor rather than being dismissed as normal self-tissue.

Moderna’s vaccine construct has room for exactly 34 neoantigens.

If you pick the wrong 34, you inject a useless sequence while the patient’s cancer returns. In the past, validating candidate targets required isolating patient blood cells and testing peptides one by one in petri dishes—a process taking 6 to 12 months.

Instead of months of manual pipetting, cloud-based machine learning pipelines evaluate thousands of genetic variants in hours. Predictive neural networks model the intracellular processing pipeline, score which mutations will stably bind the patient’s specific HLA alleles, and compile the final 34-target sequence into a single optimized mRNA string.

NoteComing Soon in Part 2: Inside the Algorithmic Compiler

How does software turn raw genomic files into a life-saving molecular sequence? In a dedicated follow-up article, we will go deep inside the machine learning stack:

  • Parsing raw FASTQ sequencing reads and denoising machine artifacts.
  • How deep neural networks trained on mass-spectrometry immunopeptidomics predict HLA presentation.
  • TCR foreignness scoring to overcome central immune tolerance.
  • Generative mRNA design: optimizing cleavable linkers, codon adaptation (CAI), and secondary RNA folding to prevent ribosomal stalling.

Beyond Melanoma: A Repeatable Platform for Oncology

The reason this Phase 3 milestone has generated so much excitement is that it is not a one-off trick for melanoma.

Melanoma was the logical starting point because its high mutational burden provided an ideal proving ground. But the underlying architecture—sequencing a tumor, running predictive neural networks, and synthesizing a multi-target mRNA construct—is a universal platform.

[Patient Biopsy (Any Solid Tumor)] ──> [Same AI Pipeline] ──> [Same mRNA Synthesis Platform] ──> [Custom Vaccine]

The exact same clinical and technological blueprint is already being tested in ongoing trials:

  • Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: The Phase 3 INTerpath-002 trial is actively evaluating the same platform in resected lung cancer.
  • Other Solid Tumors: Additional trials are exploring individualized mRNA therapies in bladder, renal cell (kidney), and pancreatic cancers.

The Next Frontier: Scaling Manufacturing

The computational models run in hours; the remaining industrial challenge is physical scaling.

Traditional pharmaceutical manufacturing is built around large-batch economy of scale: making thousands of identical doses in a single massive bioreactor. Individualized neoantigen therapy requires manufacturing—thousands of unique, small-scale synthesis runs happening in parallel, each requiring strict sterility, zero cross-contamination, and rapid release testing.

Building automated, modular manufacturing facilities that can handle tens of thousands of individualized batches every year is the operational bridge between this clinical milestone and widespread worldwide access.

The Bottom Line

For decades, the standard approach to cancer has relied on broad, non-specific interventions.

The success of the INTerpath-001 Phase 3 trial demonstrates that personalized medicine is no longer a theoretical promise. By combining high-throughput sequencing, modern machine learning, and rapid mRNA synthesis, we now have a validated method to read a patient’s individual tumor and train their own immune system to clean up what surgery left behind.

Melanoma is the first proof point. The platform being built behind it could change how we treat solid tumors for good.

Appendix & Deep-Dive Reference Guide

For clinicians, researchers, software engineers, and curious readers who want to explore the primary clinical data, foundational biology, and computational tools behind this milestone, here is a curated and annotated guide.

1. The Clinical Trial Evidence Base & Regulatory Path

  • The Pivotal Phase 3 Trial: INTerpath-001 (NCT05933577)
    • Trial Title: A Phase 3, Randomized, Double-blind, Placebo- and Active-Comparator-Controlled Study of Adjuvant V940 (mRNA-4157) Plus Pembrolizumab in Participants With Resected High-Risk (Stage IIB-IV) Melanoma.
    • Design: Enrolled ~1,089 patients across ~165 global clinical sites. Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive mRNA-4157 (1 mg IM every 3 weeks for up to 9 doses) plus pembrolizumab (200 mg IV every 3 weeks for up to 18 cycles) versus placebo plus pembrolizumab.
    • Significance: The first individualized neoantigen therapy in oncology history to hit primary and secondary endpoints in a definitive Phase 3 trial.
    • Registry: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05933577
  • The Phase 2b Proof-of-Concept: KEYNOTE-942 (The Lancet, 2024)
    • Paper: Weber, J. S., et al. “Individualised neoantigen therapy mRNA-4157 (V940) plus pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab alone in resected melanoma (KEYNOTE-942): a randomised, open-label, phase 2b trial.” The Lancet, 2024; 403(10427): 632–644. DOI: 10.1016/S0140-6736(23)02268-7.
    • Key Data: 157 patients with resected Stage IIIB–IV melanoma. Adding the mRNA vaccine reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 44% () and reduced the risk of distant metastasis or death by 65% (). Long-term follow-up presented at ASCO 2024 demonstrated durable 3-year recurrence-free survival benefits.
  • Regulatory Designations:
    • FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designation (Feb 2023): Granted by the U.S. FDA to expedite the development and review of mRNA-4157 + Keytruda for adjuvant melanoma.
    • EMA Priority Medicines (PRIME) Scheme (Apr 2023): Granted by the European Medicines Agency to accelerate regulatory access across the EU.
  • The Expanding Clinical Pipeline:
    • INTerpath-002 (NCT06077760): Phase 3 randomized study evaluating adjuvant V940 + Keytruda in completely resected Stage II, IIIA, and IIIB Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC).
    • INTerpath-004 (NCT06295809): Phase 2 trial in muscle-invasive bladder cancer / urothelial carcinoma.
    • INTerpath-005 (NCT06307431): Phase 2 trial in advanced renal cell carcinoma (kidney cancer).
    • INTerpath-007 (NCT06295822): Phase 2 trial in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC).

2. Seminal Research Papers: From Concept to Clinical Reality

  • The Neoantigen Paradigm:
    • Paper: Schumacher, T. N., & Schreiber, R. D. (2015). “Neoantigens in cancer immunotherapy.” Science, 348(6230), 69–74. DOI: 10.1126/science.aaa4971.
    • Why It Matters: The seminal paper establishing that cancer-specific somatic mutations create novel, foreign peptide flags (neoantigens) that are recognized by CD8+ and CD4+ T-cells without triggering central self-tolerance.
  • The First Personalized RNA Vaccines in Humans:
    • Paper: Sahin, U., et al. (2017). “Personalized RNA mutanome vaccines mobilize poly-specific therapeutic immunity against cancer.” Nature, 547(7662), 222–226. DOI: 10.1038/nature23003.
    • Why It Matters: Pioneering clinical proof-of-concept demonstrating that customized synthetic RNA encoding personalized somatic mutations induces de novo T-cell responses against multiple targets in advanced melanoma patients.
  • The Benchmark for Neoantigen Prediction Algorithms:
    • Paper: Wells, D. K., et al. (The TESLA Consortium) (2020). “Key Parameters of Tumor Epitope Immunogenicity Revealed by a Global Consortium for Cancer Immunotherapy.” Cell, 183(3), 818–834. DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2020.09.015.
    • Why It Matters: A landmark global benchmark comparing neoantigen prediction pipelines across 36 academic and biotech groups. Proved that simple peptide-MHC binding affinity alone generates massive false-positive rates, demonstrating why multi-model pipelines incorporating proteasomal cleavage, RNA expression weighting, and mass spectrometry presentation are mandatory.
  • Mass-Spectrometry-Driven HLA Motif Modeling:
    • Paper: Sarkizova, S., et al. (2020). “A large peptidome dataset reveals HLA class I presentation rules and enables improved peptide-MHC prediction.” Nature Biotechnology, 38(2), 199–209. DOI: 10.1038/s41587-019-0322-9.
    • Why It Matters: Established the modern foundation for training deep neural networks directly on high-throughput mass spectrometry () eluted ligand data across thousands of HLA alleles, radically improving presentation prediction accuracy over historical synthetic binding assays.
  • Molecular Mechanics of Checkpoint Blockade:
    • Paper: Ribas, A., & Wolchok, J. D. (2018). “Cancer immunotherapy using checkpoint blockade.” Science, 359(6382), 1350–1355. DOI: 10.1126/science.aar4060.
    • Why It Matters: Comprehensive review of how chronic tumor antigen stimulation drives T-cell exhaustion via the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway, and how monoclonal antibodies physically disengage this checkpoint brake.

3. Key Concepts & Clinical Mechanics Glossary

  • Complete Surgical Resection ( Resection): Removal of all macroscopic tumor tissue with microscopic margins free of malignant cells. However, an margin does not preclude the existence of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) or disseminated micrometastases in regional or distant tissue beds.
  • Dormant Micrometastases: Subclinical clusters of cancer cells that have detached from the primary lesion and lodged in distant organs. They frequently enter a state of cellular quiescence ( cell cycle arrest), evading standard imaging and conventional chemotherapies that target dividing cells, until microenvironmental cues reactivate malignant proliferation.
  • Adjuvant Therapy: Systemic treatment administered after complete surgical removal of primary disease, designed to sterilize occult micrometastatic disease and permanently prevent recurrence.
  • Recurrence-Free Survival (RFS): The time elapsed from surgical resection or study randomization until confirmed local, regional, or distant recurrence, or death from any cause.
  • Distant Metastasis-Free Survival (DMFS): The time elapsed until cancer colonizes distant organs (e.g., lungs, liver, brain, bone). In melanoma, DMFS is the single strongest clinical surrogate for Overall Survival (OS).
  • Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB): The number of non-synonymous somatic mutations per megabase (Mb) of sequenced tumor DNA. Melanoma carries one of the highest TMBs () due to ultraviolet-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer formation ( transitions), providing a dense pool of neoantigen candidates.
  • Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) System: The human Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC). Polygenic and polymorphic cell-surface glycoproteins that bind peptide fragments (8–11 amino acids for Class I; 13–17 amino acids for Class II) and display them on the cell membrane for immune surveillance by T-cell receptors.
  • Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocytes (TILs): Endogenous host immune cells (predominantly CD8+ cytolytic and CD4+ helper T-cells) that have migrated into the tumor microenvironment.
  • Lipid Nanoparticles (LNPs): Sub-100 nm synthetic spheres composed of ionizable lipids, structural phospholipids, cholesterol, and PEGylated lipids. LNPs protect synthetic mRNA from rapid enzymatic degradation by circulating ribonucleases and facilitate receptor-mediated endocytosis and endosomal escape into the cytoplasm.

4. Open-Access Computational Biology Databases & Tools

For engineers and computational biologists interested in exploring neoantigen prediction software:

  • Immune Epitope Database (IEDB): iedb.org — Free, NIAID-supported repository cataloging millions of experimentally validated epitopes, MHC binding measurements, and T-cell activation assays.
  • NetMHCpan 4.1 & NetMHCIIpan 4.0: services.healthtech.dtu.dk — Widely used pan-specific neural network tools predicting peptide binding across all known human HLA-A, -B, -C, and -DP/-DQ/-DR alleles.
  • MHCflurry 2.0: github.com/openvax/mhcflurry — Open-source deep learning framework integrating proteasomal antigen processing, TAP transport, and MHC Class I surface presentation predictors.
  • OpenVax Pipeline: github.com/openvax — An open-source suite of bioinformatics tools for variant calling, epitope prediction, and personalized vaccine design from paired tumor/normal FASTQ files.
  • UCSC Cancer Genomics Browser & TCGA: cancergenome.nih.gov — The Cancer Genome Atlas repository containing whole-exome sequencing and RNA-seq data across thousands of human tumors.

item.title: Understanding Agents and all the jargon around them from first principles
item.dc:creator: Pratyush Sinha
item.description:
Introduction

This post is about how agents work. The idea came from a blog post I was reading from Tidy Design Principles — the motivation is straightforward: cover everything you need to know to build an agent, from first principles. To keep the scope manageable, I will not touch upon how inference itself happens. That is a topic for another day.

Before we can talk about agents, we need to understand what they are built on top of: LLMs. So we will trace the evolution of LLMs — from a simple Q&A bot all the way to systems with agentic capabilities — and layer in the other concepts (tools, harnesses, caching) along the way.

Here is the roadmap:

  1. LLMs as a Q&A bot — the stateless HTTP foundation
  2. Multi-turn conversations — how context is maintained
  3. System prompts — who sets the model’s behaviour
  4. Client-side control — forking, structured output, and why you are in charge
  5. Caching — why it is expensive
  6. Tool calls — giving the LLM access to functions
  7. The harness — who actually executes those tools
  8. What is an agent? — tying it all together

The Q&A bot is the foundation everything else builds on, so we will spend the most time there.

LLMs as a Q&A Bot

When the first GPT 3.5 came out, the interaction was beautifully simple: you ask a question, you get an answer. But to understand why agents are interesting, we need to understand the mechanics of that interaction at the protocol level — specifically, how it works over HTTP.

The HTTP foundation: statelessness

The first principle to grasp is that HTTP is stateless. Every request from the client to the server is a fresh, self-contained transaction. Once the server responds, it forgets everything about you.

This has a profound implication for LLM APIs: one question can only be answered in the context of a single request. The moment that transaction completes, the server retains no memory of your prior Q&A. The next time you send a message, the server starts from scratch.

Modern LLM platforms now have session and state management layers on top, but we are not concerned with those here. We care about the core capability of the LLM API itself, and that core is stateless.

This single fact — statelessness — is the thread that explains almost every “advanced” concept that follows.

This is a trimmed version of how the API works. There is a lot that goes on and is beyond the scope of the blog.

Multi-Turn Conversations

If the server forgets everything after each response, how do you have a conversation?

The answer: the client is responsible for maintaining context. You, the client, send the entire conversation history with every new request.

Here is how it works, step by step:

  1. Turn 1: You send your first message. The server responds. Transaction over — the server forgets.
  2. Turn 2: You want to ask a follow-up. So you send both the previous user message and the previous server response (now called the assistant message), followed by your new user message. The server reads the full history and continues the conversation.

This back-and-forth — one user message paired with one assistant response — is called a turn. A conversation is a sequence of turns, and the entire sequence is resent with every request.

All of this is transmitted as JSON. The messages array in the request body contains the ordered list of {role, content} pairs. That is the entire mechanism: a growing JSON list of messages, resent each time, because the server has no memory of its own.

System Prompts

Before a single user message is sent, there is one more role to understand: the system prompt.

There are two layers here:

  1. The model provider’s system prompt. Closed-source models like Claude ship with their own internal system prompt that defines baseline behaviour, safety guidelines, and operating principles. (You can find examples of these on Anthropic’s GitHub.) Open-source models, by contrast, give you full control — there is no hidden provider prompt.

  2. Your system message. On top of the provider’s prompt, you define a system message that sets the persona, tone, and constraints for your specific use case. Think of the provider’s prompt as the constitution and your system message as the local bylaws.

So a complete message list looks like:

[system]    You are a concise assistant that speaks in bullet points.
[user]      What is the capital of France?
[assistant] Paris.
[user]      And its population?
[assistant] ...

The system message sits at the top of the list. Because the entire list is resent on every turn, the system message is effectively persistent — not because the server remembers it, but because you include it every time.

Client-Side Control: You Are in Charge

Here is a consequence of statelessness that is easy to miss: because the client controls the message list, the client controls everything.

The server never decides what context to keep or discard — you do. This unlocks several powerful patterns:

Forking

At any point in a multi-turn conversation, you can fork: take the current message list, branch off, and start a parallel conversation from that point. You can run multiple branches simultaneously and pick the one that produced the best results. You can even jump back to an earlier turn and continue from there, ignoring later messages.

The LLM has no say in this. It simply processes whatever list you hand it.

Structured output

You can ask the LLM to return its answer in a specific format — say, a JSON object with particular fields. This does not change the underlying mechanism. The response is still JSON, still part of the same message list, still resent on the next turn. Structured output is just a cleaner contract on top of the existing JSON interaction.

The takeaway

What you send to the LLM at any given point — the system message, the assistant messages, the user messages, which turns to include or skip — is entirely controlled by the client. This is not a limitation; it is a superpower.

Caching

LLM providers offer prompt caching (also called KV cache reuse): the ability to store the computed representation of a message prefix on the server side so that subsequent requests with the same prefix do not have to reprocess it from scratch. You still send the full context every turn — you simply pay less for the cached portion (often around 10% of the normal input cost).

Why is caching expensive to offer? These inference servers run in a distributed fashion across GPU machines. Maintaining state across a distributed fleet of GPU nodes — keeping KV caches resident in memory, routing subsequent requests to the same node, managing eviction — is computationally and financially costly. The server was architected to be stateless, so any persistent caching layer is an optimisation bolted on top, and providers charge accordingly.

For most use cases, you can get by without caching. It becomes important at scale, when you are re-sending large context windows on every turn.

Tool Calls

Everything so far has been pure Q&A: the LLM generates text, you consume it. The next evolutionary step is tool calls.

Consider a simple question: “Is today my anniversary?”

To answer this, the LLM needs two pieces of information:

  1. Your anniversary date — a static fact. You can include this in the system prompt or user message. No tool needed.
  2. Today’s date — dynamic information the model weights themselves do not have. The model has no built-in clock. (Some providers, like OpenAI, inject the current date into the system context for their consumer-facing products, but the raw API does not guarantee this.)

This is where tool calls come in. You define a function — say, get_today_date() in Python — and describe it to the LLM. When the LLM recognises it needs the current date, it selects that tool and signals that it wants it called. This act — the LLM choosing from a set of available tools — is called a tool call.

The critical thing to understand: the LLM does not execute the tool. It merely says, “I want to use tool X with these arguments.” The actual execution is someone else’s job.

Newer models are better at deciding when to use a tool, but the tools themselves must always be explicitly defined. Tool calls are here to stay — they are the bridge between the LLM’s text world and the real world of computation.

The Harness

So the LLM says, “Call tool X.” Who actually runs it?

You do. The execution layer that sits between the LLM’s tool-call request and the actual function invocation is called the harness.

The harness is the glue that makes tool calls real. Here is the full cycle:

  1. The user asks a question.
  2. The LLM receives the message (along with the list of available tools).
  3. The LLM decides it needs a tool and returns a tool-call request (tool name + arguments).
  4. The harness intercepts that request, executes the actual function, and collects the result.
  5. The harness feeds the result back to the LLM as a new message.
  6. The LLM digests the tool output and produces its final answer.

What the harness actually does

The description above makes the harness sound like a simple pass-through. In practice, the harness is doing a surprising amount of work at each step:

Argument validation. The LLM might return arguments that are malformed, missing required fields, or of the wrong type. The harness validates the tool-call request before executing anything. If the LLM calls get_today_date(format="dd-mm-yyyy") but your function does not accept a format parameter, the harness catches that and returns an error message to the LLM — not a crash.

Execution. The harness calls the actual function. This could be a local Python function, an HTTP call to an external API, a database query, or a shell command. The harness is agnostic to what the tool does — it just needs to run it and capture the return value.

Error handling. What happens if the function raises an exception? If the external API is down? If the database times out? The harness must catch these failures, format them as readable error messages, and feed them back to the LLM. The LLM can then decide to retry, try a different tool, or tell the user that something went wrong. Without the harness handling errors gracefully, a single API timeout would kill the entire conversation.

Serialisation. The function might return a Python object, a pandas DataFrame, a list of dicts, or raw bytes. The harness must serialise that into a string (or a JSON string) that the LLM can read. If the result is too large — say, a database query returning 10,000 rows — the harness must truncate, summarise, or paginate it. The LLM cannot digest raw binary or arbitrarily large payloads.

Logging and observability. In production, you want to know which tools were called, with what arguments, how long they took, and what they returned. The harness is the natural place to log all of this. This is not optional — when an agent misbehaves, the harness logs are how you debug it.

Security and permissions. The harness is the enforcement point. If a tool can delete files or make payments, the harness is where you add confirmation prompts, rate limits, or permission checks. The LLM should never have direct access to destructive operations — the harness mediates everything.

A concrete harness implementation

Here is what a minimal harness looks like in Python:

import json

def get_today_date():
    from datetime import date
    return date.today().isoformat()  # e.g., "2026-06-27"

def check_bank_balance():
    # In reality, this would call your bank's API
    return {"balance": 54000, "currency": "INR"}

# Registry: maps tool names to actual functions
TOOLS = {
    "get_today_date": get_today_date,
    "check_bank_balance": check_bank_balance,
}

def run_harness(tool_call):
    """Execute a single tool-call request from the LLM."""
    name = tool_call["name"]
    args = tool_call.get("arguments", {})

    # 1. Validate: does this tool exist?
    if name not in TOOLS:
        return json.dumps({"error": f"Unknown tool: {name}"})

    func = TOOLS[name]

    # 2. Execute with error handling
    try:
        result = func(**args)
    except TypeError as e:
        # Argument mismatch
        return json.dumps({"error": f"Invalid arguments: {e}"})
    except Exception as e:
        # Any other failure
        return json.dumps({"error": f"Tool execution failed: {e}"})

    # 3. Serialise
    if isinstance(result, str):
        return result
    return json.dumps(result)

And here is how the harness is called in the loop:

# The LLM returned a tool-call request
tool_call = {"name": "get_today_date", "arguments": {}}

# The harness executes it
tool_result = run_harness(tool_call)  # returns "2026-06-27"

# The harness result is appended to the message list
messages.append({
    "role": "tool",
    "name": "get_today_date",
    "content": tool_result
})

# The updated message list is sent back to the LLM

The harness is your code. You write it. It is the cycle of “LLM says do X → you validate X → you execute X → you handle errors → you serialise the result → you tell the LLM what happened → LLM continues.”

What Is an Agent?

Now we can define an agent clearly.

An agent is a client-side loop that places the LLM inside an autonomous cycle. Instead of a single question-and-answer, the agent:

  1. Evaluates the user’s goal.
  2. Determines a sequence of actions (which tools to call, in what order).
  3. Calls the harness to execute each action.
  4. Observes the results.
  5. Loops until the objective is met.

In the simplest terms: an agent is a harness wrapped in a loop. The harness handles a single tool-call cycle; the agent orchestrates many such cycles, driving toward a goal the user stated once.

The anatomy of an agent loop

A minimal agent loop in pseudocode:

def run_agent(user_goal, tools, system_prompt):
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
        {"role": "user",   "content": user_goal}
    ]

    while True:
        # 1. Call the LLM with the current message list + tool definitions
        response = llm.chat(messages, tools=tools)

        # 2. Did the LLM return a tool call, or a final answer?
        if response.has_tool_call():
            # 3. Harness executes the tool
            result = run_harness(response.tool_call)
            # 4. Feed the result back to the LLM
            messages.append({
                "role": "tool",
                "content": result
            })
            # Loop continues — LLM will be called again
        else:
            # 5. LLM produced a final answer — we are done
            return response.content

That is the entire skeleton. Every agent framework — LangChain, CrewAI, OpenAI Assistants, Claude Code — is a variation on this while True loop with different amounts of scaffolding around it.

What separates a toy agent from a production agent

The loop above is deceptively simple. In practice, production agents add several layers on top:

Planning. Instead of blindly calling tools one at a time, a good agent first generates a plan. It breaks the user’s goal into sub-tasks and works through them deliberately. This is not magic — the “plan” is just the LLM producing a structured list of steps in its response, which the agent then follows.

State tracking (to-do lists). As the agent works through a multi-step task, it needs to track what it has done and what remains. A common pattern: the LLM generates a to-do list at the start, updates it after each step (marking items complete, adding new ones as it discovers them), and uses it to decide what to do next. This is exactly how Claude Code operates — you can watch it generate and update a checklist as it works.

Termination conditions. The while True loop needs an exit condition. Options include: the LLM explicitly says “I am done” (returns a response with no tool call), a maximum number of iterations is reached (to prevent infinite loops), or a token/time budget is exhausted. Getting this right is critical — an agent that never terminates is a bug, not a feature.

Human-in-the-loop checkpoints. For high-stakes actions (deploying code, making a payment, deleting files), the agent should pause and ask the user for confirmation before the harness executes the tool. Claude Code does this in its plan mode — it presents what it intends to do, asks for approval, and only then proceeds to execute.

Error recovery. When a tool call fails (API timeout, permission denied, invalid input), a production agent does not just crash. The LLM reads the error message, reasons about what went wrong, and tries an alternative approach — a different tool, different arguments, or asking the user for help.

How Claude Code does it: a real-world agent in action

Claude Code is one of the most transparent examples of an agent loop in production. When you give it a task like “refactor the authentication module and add tests,” here is what happens:

  1. Plan mode. Claude Code first enters a planning phase. It reads the relevant files (using its read_file tool), understands the codebase, and generates a plan: “I will create a new AuthManager class, update the three files that depend on the old module, and write unit tests.” It presents this plan to the user and asks for confirmation before doing anything.

  2. To-do generation. Once approved, it creates a structured to-do list — not in its head, but as an explicit artefact you can see in the terminal:

  3. Execution loop. It works through the to-do list one item at a time. For each item, it may call multiple tools: read_file to understand a dependency, write_file to create the new class, run_tests to verify the change, grep to find all references to the old module. Each tool call goes through the harness — Claude Code executes the function, captures the output, and feeds it back to the LLM.

  4. To-do updates. After completing each item, it marks it done (✓) and sometimes adds new items it discovered along the way (e.g., “fix broken import in utils.py that I noticed while editing routes/login.py”).

  5. Verification. Before declaring the task complete, it runs the test suite one more time and summarises what it did. If tests fail, it loops back — reads the error, edits the code, re-runs tests — until everything passes or it asks the user for help.

This entire sequence is the agent loop: plan → generate to-do → execute step → observe result → update to-do → execute next step → … → verify → done. Every single action — reading a file, writing code, running tests — is a harness cycle. Claude Code is just a very well-engineered while loop around that harness, with planning and state tracking layered on top.

The takeaway

The most minimal agent you can think of might have just a handful of tools — read a file, search code, run a command — and loop until the task is done. Systems like OpenAI’s Codex agent, Devin, and Claude Code are elaborate instances of this same pattern, but the skeleton is always the same: LLM + tools + harness + loop = agent. What separates a toy from production is not a different architecture — it is the quality of planning, state tracking, error recovery, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints layered on top of that same loop.

Putting It All Together: A Worked Example

To make everything concrete, let us trace a single scenario end to end. We will follow one example through every concept we have covered — statelessness, multi-turn context, system prompts, client-side control, tool calls, the harness, and the agent loop.

The scenario

You have a monthly SIP of ₹15,000 that gets auto-debited on the 5th of every month. You want your assistant to answer: “How many days until my next SIP payment is due?”

The SIP due date (5th of every month) and the amount (₹15,000) are static facts. But the current date is dynamic — the LLM does not know it. So we will need a tool.

Let us walk through this in stages, labelling the component that is active at each step.

Stage 1 — The system prompt

Before any user message, you set the system message. This defines the persona and the ground rules:

[
  {
    "role": "system",
    "content": "You are a personal finance assistant for Indian users. You help track SIPs, EMIs, and bill payments. If you need dynamic information (like today's date), use the get_today_date tool. If you need to check the user's bank balance, use the check_bank_balance tool. The user has a monthly SIP of ₹15,000 auto-debited on the 5th of every month."
  }
]

Component active: System prompt. The static facts (SIP amount, due date) are baked in here. The model provider’s own system prompt sits above this and is not shown — it governs baseline safety and behaviour.

Stage 2 — The user asks a question (Turn 1)

The user sends their message. The client appends it to the message list:

[
  {"role": "system",    "content": "You are a personal finance assistant for Indian users. ..."},
  {"role": "user",      "content": "How many days until my next SIP payment is due?"}
]

This entire list is sent to the LLM API over HTTP.

Component active: Stateless HTTP + multi-turn context. The server has never seen this user before. Everything the LLM knows comes from this single JSON payload. If this were Turn 2, the list would also contain the previous assistant message — that is how context is maintained.

Stage 3 — The LLM recognises it needs a tool

The LLM reads the system prompt, sees the SIP is due on the 5th, and realises it needs today’s date to compute the difference. It does not guess or hallucinate a date. Instead, it returns a tool-call request:

[
  {
    "role": "assistant",
    "tool_calls": [
      {
        "name": "get_today_date",
        "arguments": {}
      }
    ]
  }
]

Component active: Tool call. The LLM chose a tool from the set you defined. It did not execute anything — it merely signalled, “I need to call get_today_date.” The tool definition (name, description, expected parameters) was provided by you alongside the message list when you made the API request.

Stage 4 — The harness executes the tool

The client-side code — the harness — intercepts the tool-call request. It validates the arguments (empty, which is fine since get_today_date takes none), runs the actual Python function, and captures the result:

def get_today_date():
    from datetime import date
    return date.today().isoformat()  # e.g., "2026-06-27"

The harness gets the result ("2026-06-27"), serialises it into a string, and appends it to the message list as a new message with the role tool:

[
  {"role": "system",    "content": "You are a personal finance assistant for Indian users. ..."},
  {"role": "user",      "content": "How many days until my next SIP payment is due?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": null, "tool_calls": [{"name": "get_today_date", "arguments": {}}]},
  {"role": "tool",      "name": "get_today_date", "content": "2026-06-27"}
]

Component active: Harness. This is your code. You validated the arguments, you executed the function, you serialised the output, and you captured any errors. The LLM had no part in this execution. The harness then sends this updated message list back to the LLM for the next step.

Stage 5 — The LLM produces the final answer (Turn 1 completes)

The LLM now sees the full picture: the SIP is due on the 5th, today is the 27th of June, so the next payment is July 5th. It computes the difference and responds:

[
  {"role": "system",    "content": "You are a personal finance assistant for Indian users. ..."},
  {"role": "user",      "content": "How many days until my next SIP payment is due?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": null, "tool_calls": [{"name": "get_today_date", "arguments": {}}]},
  {"role": "tool",      "name": "get_today_date", "content": "2026-06-27"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "Your next SIP payment of ₹15,000 is due on July 5th. That is 8 days from today."}
]

Component active: Multi-turn context. Notice how the entire history — system prompt, user question, tool-call request, tool result, and final answer — is now one growing list. If the user asks a follow-up (“Can I reschedule it?”), this entire list is resent. The server still remembers nothing on its own.

Stage 6 — What if the user follows up? (Turn 2 and client-side control)

The user asks: “Can you also check whether I have enough balance for the SIP this month?”

You, the client, decide what to include in the next request. You could:

  • Send everything — the full list above plus the new user message. The LLM sees the entire conversation and knows the SIP is ₹15,000 due on July 5th.
  • Fork — branch off from Stage 2 with a different question, ignoring the SIP conversation entirely.
  • Prune — drop the tool-call messages and only keep the system prompt + final assistant answer + new user message. The LLM would still know the answer (₹15,000 on July 5th) but would not know a tool was ever called.

Component active: Client-side control. The server never decides what context to keep. You do. You could even start a completely separate conversation with a different system prompt — the LLM has no idea these two conversations are related.

Stage 7 — What makes this an agent?

In the example above, there was one tool call, one harness execution, and one final answer. That is a harness cycle — a single loop iteration.

An agent is what happens when you wrap this in an autonomous loop. Imagine the user says: “Check if my SIP payment is due this week, and if so, check my bank balance and tell me if I have enough to cover it.”

Now the LLM must: 1. Call get_today_date → harness validates, executes, returns June 27th. 2. Reason: the 5th is next week, SIP is ₹15,000 → call check_bank_balance → harness validates, executes, returns ₹54,000. 3. Reason: ₹15,000 ≤ ₹54,000 → produce final answer: “Your SIP of ₹15,000 is due on July 5th (8 days away) and your balance is ₹54,000. You have sufficient funds.”

Each step is a harness cycle. The agent is the outer loop that keeps cycling — LLM reasons → selects tool → harness executes → feed result back → LLM reasons again — until the user’s goal is fully met.

Component active: Agent loop. The agent is not a new API feature. It is a client-side while loop around the harness: “keep going until the LLM says it is done.”

Recap: which component does what

Component What it does Who controls it
System prompt Sets persona, static facts, and ground rules You (the client)
Message list The full conversation history, resent every turn You (the client)
Tool call The LLM’s decision to use a function The LLM
Harness Executes the function and feeds the result back You (the client)
Agent loop Cycles LLM → tool → harness → LLM until the goal is met You (the client)

The LLM’s only real power is choosing which tool to call and reasoning about the results. Everything else — the context, the execution, the loop — is your code. That is what “client-side” means, and that is why the harness and the agent loop are not part of the LLM itself.

Tool Implications: Where We Go From Here

With this foundation in place — statelessness, multi-turn context, system prompts, client-side control, tool calls, harnesses, and the agent loop — a lot of the popular jargon in the AI space becomes much easier to parse. Many “advanced” concepts are just combinations of the primitives we have covered here.

In the next posts, we will dive deeper into specific agent architectures and real-world implementations.

item.title: HBR On Managing Yourself: Purpose, Strengths & Reclaiming Work (Part 1 of 2)
item.dc:creator: Pratyush Sinha
item.description:
Managing Your Career Trajectory in the AI Era (HBR Series - Part 1 of 2)

This was the author’s first book from the HBR series. The book is a collection of articles on how one can manage oneself, offering different points of view int/modelended primarily for managers at all levels, though many of the ideas feel equally relevant in the age of AI. The summaries below draw largely from the “Idea in Brief” and “Idea in Practice” sections of each chapter. Several of the articles come across as especially sharp and relevant, and the book itself feels approachable rather than dense.

How Will You Measure Your Life?

How will you measure your life?

It starts off with a broad set of three questions: - How can I be sure that I will be happy in my career? This question arose from Frederick Herzberg’s assertion that the most powerful motivator isn’t money; it is the opportunity to learn, grow in responsibilities, contribute, and be recognized. - How can I ensure that my relationship with my spouse and my family becomes an enduring source of happiness? - How can I be sure I will stay out of jail? The article argues for having a clear sense of purpose; without it, people are likely to fritter away time and energy chasing the most tangible signs of achievement rather than what is truly important. A focus on marginal gains can lead people astray. The marginal cost of doing something wrong “just this once” always seems alluringly low, but you do not see the end result to which that path leads. The key is to define what you stand for and draw the line in a safe place.

Create a Strategy for Life

Allocate Resources: Align your actual spending of time, talent, and energy with your stated priorities.

Create a Culture: Designing a deliberate culture sets you up for the long term.

It is one thing to look into a foggy future with acuity and chart the course corrections that a company must make, but quite another to persuade employees, who might not see the changes ahead, to line up and work cooperatively to take the company in a new direction. For organizations, this alignment depends on two separate dimensions: 1. The extent to which members of the organization agree on what they want from their participation in the enterprise. 2. The extent to which they agree on which actions will produce the desired results.

Critical Takeaways

  • Avoid the marginal costs mistake: It is easier to hold to your principles 100% of the time than it is to hold to them 98% of the time.
  • Remember the importance of humility: The most humble people generally have a high level of self-esteem. They know who they are and they feel good about who they are. Humility is not defined by self-deprecating behavior or attitudes, but by the esteem with which a person regards others. True humbleness unlocks the opportunity to learn a lot from everyone around you.
  • Choosing the right yardstick: In the end, resolve to measure your life by the individuals you have touched and the people you have helped become better. ## Personal Note: What stood out most to me was the idea of intentionally creating a culture, especially the parallel between organizational culture and a family’s own culture at home. The article’s strongest takeaways for me were the importance of avoiding the marginal cost mistake and practicing humility in its truest sense.

Managing Oneself

Managing Oneself ## Part 1: Finding Your Strengths & Managing Yourself

Discovering Your Strengths through Feedback Analysis

  • The Method: Whenever you make a key decision or take a key action, write down what you expect will happen. Compare the actual results with your expectations 9 to 12 months later.
  • The Timeline: Practicing this consistently for 2 to 3 years will clearly identify where your strengths lie.
  • The Outcome: This method reveals what you are doing (or failing to do) that deprives you of the full benefits of your strengths, and clearly highlights areas where you lack competence. ### Acting on the Analysis
  • Concentrate on your strengths and place yourself where they can produce maximum results.
  • Work continuously on improving your strengths and acquiring new skills as identified by the analysis.
  • Overcome Intellectual Arrogance: Do not let expertise in one area breed contempt for other fields. Being bright is never a substitute for actual knowledge.

Part 2: The Core Questions for an Excellent Life

To build a life of excellence, you must deeply understand the answers to these five questions: 1. What are my strengths? (Discovered via feedback analysis) 2. How do I work? - Do you process information best by reading or by listening/discussing? - Do you accomplish more working with others, or working alone? - Do you perform best as a decision-maker, or as an advisor on key matters? - Do you thrive under stress, or do you function optimally in a highly predictable environment? 3. What are my values? - What are your ethics and your most important responsibilities for living a worthy life? - Note: If your organization’s ethics do not resonate with your own values, your career will likely be marked by frustration and poor performance. 4. Where do I belong? - Combine your strengths, work style, and values to find the right environment. Fitting into the right environment transforms you from an acceptable employee into a star performer. 5. What can I contribute? - Instead of waiting to be told what to do, look at what the situation requires and decide how you can make the greatest organizational impact based on your strengths, style, and values.

Part 3: Responsibility for Relationships

Achieving anything meaningful requires working effectively with others. Managing yourself means taking full responsibility for relationships, which consists of two parts: - Accepting Individual Differences: Accept that your co-workers are individuals who will insist on behaving like human beings. They have their own strengths, values, and ways of getting things done. To be effective, you must learn and respect how they work. - Taking Responsibility for Communication: Most personality clashes in organizations happen because people do not know what others are doing, how they do it, or what results they expect. The remedy is simple: you must communicate and ask — ## Part 4: Managing the Second Half of Your Life As careers elongate, the “second half” of life (spanning 20 to 25 years) requires preparation long before you actually enter it. By the time many executives reach a stable point in their careers or stop climbing the corporate ladder, they need a secondary source of fulfillment. Developing this early ensures you can navigate major setbacks and keep growing. ### Three Ways to Introduce a Second Career 1. Moving Organizations: This involves taking a second career by simply moving from one type of organization to another. 2. Developing a Parallel Career: Staying in your primary job (full-time, part-time, or consulting) while simultaneously creating or joining a non-profit organization. 3. Social Entrepreneurship: For those who have been highly successful in their first jobs and choose to pivot into social entrepreneurship, continuing to use their lifelong skills but shifting their primary focus toward social impact. There are two ways to prepare for the second half of your life—actually, there are three. The first one is nothing more than moving from one kind of organization to another. This is practically taking a second career. The second way to prepare for the second half of life is to develop a parallel career. Many people who are very successful in the first half stay in the work they have been doing, either on a full-time or part-time or consulting basis, but in addition, they create or join a non-profit organization. The third kind of people are those who have been very successful in their first jobs, and that’s when they decide that they want to enter social entrepreneurship, doing what they have been doing all along, but spending less time on it.

Personal Note:

Re-Inventing the Professional Self: Reflections on Managing Oneself in the Era of AI

I have often approached personal growth with the urgency of a 90-day sprint. When I previously tracked my decisions, I expected clear patterns and definitive results within three months, which led to frustration when progress was not obvious. Reading this reshaped that perspective. Realizing that feedback analysis is a steady 2-to-3-year discipline gave me permission to shift from chasing instant validation to committing to a longer practice of tracking my strengths, noticing where intellectual arrogance creates blind spots, and identifying where I truly excel. ### The Evolution of a Software Career in the AI Age From early on, and later in college, my path toward software became clear. Even then, however, I carried a quiet belief that I would not do software forever. I always sensed the need for a second act—some future space to step back, reflect, and pivot. Today, that instinct feels especially relevant. As AI rapidly changes the landscape for knowledge workers, waiting until the literal “second half of life” to reinvent oneself no longer feels realistic. AI is not only changing tools; it is accelerating the need to think seriously about alternate or parallel careers much earlier than previous generations did. This article reinforced for me that reinvention is not a reckless gamble but a recurring pattern in professional life. People have done this before. For me, developing a parallel career—perhaps in the non-profit or social entrepreneurship space while continuing to work in tech—is not merely a hedge against AI automation. It is a practical way to continue growing, learning, and staying relevant. ### Navigating Work Style: Readers vs. Listeners One of my most meaningful takeaways was the distinction between readers and listeners. It felt like a subtle but profound behavioral truth. Understanding whether someone processes the world best through written material or through discussion has a major impact on how that person should position themselves. It also helps explain why some environments feel natural while others feel draining, and why performance under pressure can vary so much. ### The Missing Piece: Responsibility for Relationships Looking back on my career so far, the section on responsibility for relationships resonated deeply. I keep seeing two missing elements in professional life: 1. Accepting Individual Differences: Internalizing that coworkers are individuals who will insist on being human, each with their own strengths, values, and ways of getting things done. 2. Taking Responsibility for Communication: Recognizing that many so-called personality clashes are not truly about personality at all. They happen because people do not ask what others are doing, how they work, or what results they expect.

For me, managing oneself means actively working to bridge that communication gap, even when others are not yet doing the same. ### A Mature Perspective

I believe I would not have appreciated this article in the same way when I was younger. It takes time in the trenches—feeling the friction of corporate life and witnessing technological change firsthand—to fully value these insights. For me, the article served as a reminder that some things simply take time, and that it is better to be patient and consistent than to chase quick wins.

Reclaim Your Job

Many managers waste time and erode their productivity by grappling with an endless list of demands from others. The article questions why people so often assume those demands are fixed requirements, and how the absence of discussion allows those demands to control their jobs. As a result, many remain trapped in inefficiency. The way out is to recognize opportunities, trust one’s own judgment, and pursue personal goals methodically. To align organizational objectives, priorities, and supporting effort, people must overcome resource constraints by attacking goals strategically, demonstrating success step by step, and developing alternatives to use when Plan A fails. The larger promise of the article is that people can make a real difference in their organizations while also building satisfying careers by understanding how they inhibit themselves from strategic action. They can seize control of their jobs rather than letting their jobs control them. The payoff is impressive results for the company and more rewarding work lives.

Idea in Practice

To reclaim your job and better support your company’s practice, apply three strategies: 1. Prioritize demands to achieve personal and organizational goals quickly. Slow down, and focus your time and attention. 2. Liberate resources to ease resource constraints and secure the backing you need. Attack your goals strategically and be patient; the process can take years. 3. Exploit alternatives, using your expertise to speed past and circumvent potential obstacles to the scope of opportunity for your company and yourself.

Personal Note:

This is a very short article, but it stood out to me because of how effectively it used concrete examples to show how goals can be pursued while also building a durable career. I was especially impressed by how concise, focused, and well-directed the article was.
